item.title: Listener Emails on Meta Glasses, Luna AI, Runa TTS and Braille Pricing
item.dc:creator: Double Tap
item.description: Should blind and low vision users install iOS 27 right away? Steven Scott and Shaun Preece explain why VoiceOver users might wait a month. Then they open the inbox for listener emails on Meta glasses problems, the best smart glasses for reading, Luna AI, Siri dictation and the high cost of Braille displays.
item.content:encoded:
Should blind and low vision users install iOS 27 right away? Steven Scott and Shaun Preece explain why VoiceOver users might wait a month. Then they open the inbox for listener emails on Meta glasses problems, the best smart glasses for reading, Luna AI, Siri dictation and the high cost of Braille displays.

Steven’s yearly advice to hold off on iOS 27 got some pushback online, and the hosts explain the reasoning. If VoiceOver breaks, a blind user loses their screen. They cover reports of tinny speech, why the nerds should test first, and hidden code that could let Claude sit behind the Siri AI interface. They also get into cluttered screen reader navigation on Facebook and LinkedIn.

Dan in Preston says Meta glasses in the UK have stopped doing look and tell. Shaun has hit the same bug and shares a workaround. Steven gives an update on his locked Microsoft account. Donnie from Oklahoma wants to know whether the AGIGA EchoVision or Meta glasses read print better, which leads to a chat about Envision, OOrion and Google’s glasses coming this fall.

Lena recommends Luna AI, an accessible voice tutor, and Shane in St. John’s, Newfoundland gives Siri’s new advanced dictation high marks, with one exception. Cheryl enjoys the Nicky voice for Kindle books. That sparks a look at Runa TTS pronunciation quirks and Stash and Jot, two apps Steven built with Claude. Leander closes by calling for payment plans, leasing or subscriptions to make Braille displays affordable.

item.title: Is AI Really That Dangerous? Will Guyatt Joins, Plus First Thoughts on Siri AI
item.dc:creator: Double Tap
item.description: Is the AI industry sounding a real alarm, or is it about money? Tech journalist Will Guyatt joins Steven Scott and Shaun Preece to make sense of the AI pause warnings. Then it's a first look at Siri AI in the iOS 27 beta and a candid chat about Windows, the Mac and screen readers.
item.content:encoded:
Is the AI industry sounding a real alarm, or is it about money? Tech journalist Will Guyatt joins Steven Scott and Shaun Preece to make sense of the AI pause warnings. Then it’s a first look at Siri AI in the iOS 27 beta and a candid chat about Windows, the Mac and screen readers.

Will lays out three theories behind a chaotic news week. AI makers could be alarmed by how quickly their models are moving. Donald Trump wants no brakes in a race with China. Or AI companies short on funding may be delaying their IPOs and reshaping the story. He also points listeners to Ed Zitron, a sceptic of the AI business model.

Steven and Shaun then weigh up what “AI will kill humanity” really means. They cover rogue AI agents, an email assistant that forwarded a message nobody asked it to send, AI tools given credit cards, and why government regulation may be too slow to matter.

The mood lifts with hands-on impressions of Siri AI in the iOS 27 public beta, including the waiting list, the Dynamic Island and early bugs. There’s a reminder to hold off on updating your daily phone, because banking apps and third-party apps may break, plus an inaccessible Barclays app.

The episode closes with Creative USB speakers that switch audio back to the laptop, and why Windows with NVDA or JAWS feels more logical than the Mac. Plans to learn grade 2 braille and use a webcam to give Claude eyes round things off.

35:18 – Why to wait before updating, and banking apps

51:33 – Giving Claude eyes and final thoughts

item.title: Mainstream: Marc Aflalo’s Take On Apple’s ‘Surprise And Shine’ Event
item.dc:creator: Double Tap
item.description: Apple's Surprise and Shine event brought the foldable iPhone Duo, AirPods 5 and a quiet RAM boost for Apple Watch Ultra 4. Steven Scott and Marc Aflalo of YourTechReport pick out what matters, what could have been a press release, and whether the Duo can replace an iPad for someone who travels a lot.
item.content:encoded:
Apple’s Surprise and Shine event brought the foldable iPhone Duo, AirPods 5 and a quiet RAM boost for Apple Watch Ultra 4. Steven Scott and Marc Aflalo of YourTechReport pick out what matters, what could have been a press release, and whether the Duo can replace an iPad for someone who travels a lot.

Steven found most of the keynote boring. Marc liked more of it, starting with Live Rewind, which lets your Apple Watch catch the last 15 seconds of a conversation you missed. That raises questions about privacy, where the data lives, and why features like the expressive Siri AI voices leave out the iPhone 15 Pro. They also look at the Ultra 4 going from 2GB to 4GB of RAM, and Steven explains why VoiceOver has felt sluggish on his Ultra 3.

AirPods 5 bring active noise cancellation to the $129 model with no ear tips, and the wireless charging version adds volume control on the stem. Marc describes how the AirPods hearing features help him focus in noisy restaurants. Steven makes the case for wired USB-C EarPods when VoiceOver latency matters.

Then the iPhone Duo. Marc expects to buy one, because a 7.6-inch inner screen could let him leave his iPad at home. They cover the passport-sized design, Touch ID, the under-screen camera, MagSafe, and a closed thickness of around 11.2mm. iPhone Handoff, which lets two iPhones share one number, leaves open questions about carriers and cost.

The conversation ends on whether a Pro Duo is coming, why the iPhone Air will probably survive, and why the 17e is still a sensible pick for many buyers.

1:44 – Live Rewind, audio intelligence and privacy
3:21 – Which devices get Siri AI features
4:36 – Apple Watch Ultra 4 RAM and the Series 12

12:52 – iPhone Duo first impressions and design
19:01 – iPhone Handoff and sharing one number
22:32 – MagSafe, cases and unconfirmed specs
24:18 – A Pro Duo, the iPhone Air and what to buy

item.title: Weekend Classic: Honda Cynic
item.dc:creator: Double Tap
item.description: Honda Scenic Audio set out to describe the view from a car window for blind and visually impaired passengers, using computer vision and generative AI. Steven Scott and Shaun Preece revisit their 2024 conversation about the app, built with Perkins School for the Blind, and ask whether poetic AI scenery description is something blind people actually want.
item.content:encoded:
Honda Scenic Audio set out to describe the view from a car window for blind and visually impaired passengers, using computer vision and generative AI. Steven Scott and Shaun Preece revisit their 2024 conversation about the app, built with Perkins School for the Blind, and ask whether poetic AI scenery description is something blind people actually want.

This episode is supported by Pneuma Solutions. Creators of accessible tools like Remote Incident Manager and Scribe. Find out more at https://pneumasolutions.com/

Honda announced Scenic Audio in April 2024 as a beta. You hold your phone to the window, it works in any car, and it narrates the passing landscape in storytelling language instead of practical directions. Steven thinks back to a Rocky Mountaineer train journey from Banff to Vancouver where he’d have loved more description. Shaun wonders what it would make of an ordinary drive through town.

Shaun’s bigger question is whether true real-time description exists yet. Steven points to the Be My Eyes demo of GPT-4o describing ducks on a pond, and argues this app sits alongside tools like Be My AI and Google Lookout.

Phil Hruska of Honda explains how the project grew out of Honda’s focus on inclusivity, with guidance from Dr. Josh Loebner, who is blind himself, on involving disabled people from the start. Sandy Lacey of the Howe Innovation Center describes interviews with around 30 blind and low vision people, and why testers enjoyed details they hadn’t realised they were missing. The Alabama Institute for Deaf and Blind and Honda’s Enable associate group also took part in beta testing.

Honda’s R&D history comes up too, from ASIMO to office chairs that move out of your way, along with Shaun’s wish for self-driving wheelie bins. Back in 2026, the hosts reflect on how much AI tools have changed since this was recorded.

Chapters

2:38 – Honda Scenic Audio explained
3:51 – Honda’s launch video
5:27 – Would you use it? Scenic trips and everyday drives
8:12 – Real-time description and the Be My Eyes GPT-4o comparison
11:54 – The Honda and Perkins partnership with Phil Hruska
16:07 – Listening to blind users and Honda’s R&D projects
19:56 – What testers said about the app
22:46 – The verdict: Honda Cynic
25:43 – Looking back from 2026

Be My Eyes: https://www.bemyeyes.com

item.title: Audio Description For Sighted People, Clipman Updates, and the AI Extinction Story
item.dc:creator: Double Tap
item.description: Audio description was built for blind and partially sighted viewers. RNIB brought broadcasters to London to ask whether sighted audiences want it too, and what that would change for the rest of us. Steven Scott reports back from the Audio Is King event, before the show turns to Clipman, an Audacity 4 warning, and the Anthropic resignation that put AI extinction talk on every front page.
item.content:encoded:
Audio description was built for blind and partially sighted viewers. RNIB brought broadcasters to London to ask whether sighted audiences want it too, and what that would change for the rest of us. Steven Scott reports back from the Audio Is King event, before the show turns to Clipman, an Audacity 4 warning, and the Anthropic resignation that put AI extinction talk on every front page.

RNIB surveyed more than 1,200 sighted people and found roughly 42 percent already knew what audio description is. Steven and Shaun compare that with audiobooks, which stayed a small shelf of expensive CD boxsets until Audible made them mainstream and quality improved for everyone. The same could happen with description, listened to on a commute or at the gym, if discovery improves. Shaun argues the real barrier is presentation: burying it in a languages menu keeps it hidden, and the name itself may need rethinking. Described video, the term used in Canada, came up as a clearer alternative.

Behind the slow progress sits a familiar problem. Accessibility teams inside broadcasters are small, and every department arrives at the priorities meeting asking where the value is. Steven makes the case that description could be an offering rather than a cost, pointing to companion podcasts, to what television could learn from audio-first storytelling, and to AMI’s integrated described video, where the script carries the picture instead of a separate voice. He also pays tribute to Sonali Rai at RNIB and to audio describer Marie Campbell, whose voice Steven recognised live on stage.

Two warnings follow. Audacity 4 rebuilds the interface in Qt and, in testing, screen reader access is badly broken, so stay on the version you have. New iOS and macOS releases land next week, and the advice is to wait a month and read the AppleVis bug report first. On a brighter note, Clipman from Andre Louis now runs on Linux and offers a self-hosted server, so encrypted clipboard sync works across Windows, Mac, Android and iPhone without a cloud account.

The episode closes on Jacob Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic this week saying neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is acting responsibly and that both are racing toward self-improving superintelligence. Colleagues publicly agreed the risk is real. Steven and Shaun weigh how seriously to take percentage odds on human extinction, why biological weapons and infrastructure hacking changed the shape of the fear, and why the story has been met with near silence inside the blind tech community.

Chapters
0:00 – Please don’t kill us all
0:19 – RNIB’s Audio Is King event and audio description for sighted audiences
24:32 – Clipman gains Linux support and a self-hosted server
29:08 – Do not install Audacity 4
33:14 – New iOS and macOS updates: wait a month
35:52 – Jacob Coxon resigns from Anthropic

Relevant Links

Clipman by Andre Louis: https://github.com/OnjLouis/Clipman
AMI: https://www.ami.ca

item.title: Introducing Double Tap Live
item.dc:creator: Double Tap
item.description: Introducing Double Tap Live. A 24/7 streaming audio channel dedicated to accessibility, assistive technology and disability inclusion. Always on. Launching Wednesday, September 30 at 1pm Eastern.
item.content:encoded:
Introducing Double Tap Live. A 24/7 streaming audio channel dedicated to accessibility, assistive technology and disability inclusion. Always on. Launching Wednesday, September 30 at 1pm Eastern.

Double Tap Live opens with a two-hour live celebration marking ten years of Double Tap, with announcements about what comes next. It’s the first in a new monthly live series with listener call-ins, special features and guests.

Kicking it off: Sriram Ganesh, founder and CEO of Lumin, the voice-first AI assistant built for blind and low vision users, joins Steven Scott and Shaun Preece for an Ask Me Anything.

Send your questions to feedback@doubletaponair.com

Once live, the channel runs around the clock: original shows including Double Tap Presents: Good Vibes and Our Perspective, partner podcasts, interviews, live event coverage from CES and accessibility conferences worldwide, and monthly live call-in shows.

HOW TO LISTEN

About Double Tap
Hosted by the insightful duo, Steven Scott and Shaun Preece, Double Tap is a treasure trove of information for anyone who’s blind or partially sighted and has a passion for tech. Steven and Shaun not only demystify tech, but they also regularly feature interviews and welcome guests from the community, fostering an interactive and engaging environment. Tune in every day of the week, and you’ll discover how technology can seamlessly integrate into your life, enhancing daily tasks and experiences, even if your sight is limited.
